title: NCLEX: Lab Values and Vital Signs
description: For nursing exam learners reviewing adult lab values, vital signs, and interpretation in common US reporting units. Ranges vary between references and laboratories; verify with current guidelines.

sources.name: Original questions from standard nursing knowledge
Open RN Health Alterations: Appendix A reference ranges

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Serum sodium?
cards.back: 135-145 mEq/L. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: Which electrolyte is the principal extracellular cation?
cards.back: Sodium; its concentration reflects water balance relative to sodium, not simply total body sodium.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Serum potassium?
cards.back: 3.5-5.0 mEq/L. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: Why are major potassium abnormalities a cardiac concern?
cards.back: Potassium affects cardiac electrical activity; both low and high levels can cause dangerous dysrhythmias.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Serum chloride?
cards.back: 98-106 mEq/L. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: Which major extracellular anion helps maintain electrical neutrality?
cards.back: Chloride; it also participates in fluid and acid-base balance.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Serum total CO2 on a chemistry panel?
cards.back: About 22-29 mEq/L. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: What does total CO2 on a routine chemistry panel mainly represent?
cards.back: Bicarbonate; this is different from arterial carbon dioxide partial pressure.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Total serum calcium?
cards.back: About 8.5-10.5 mg/dL. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: How can low albumin affect total calcium?
cards.back: It can lower total calcium without a corresponding fall in biologically active ionized calcium.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Ionized calcium?
cards.back: About 4.5-5.6 mg/dL. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: Which calcium measurement reflects the biologically active fraction?
cards.back: Ionized calcium, the unbound fraction; its level is also influenced by blood pH.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Serum magnesium?
cards.back: About 1.7-2.2 mg/dL. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: Why may low potassium persist when magnesium is low?
cards.back: Magnesium deficiency can promote renal potassium loss, making hypokalemia difficult to correct.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Adult serum phosphorus?
cards.back: About 2.5-4.5 mg/dL. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: What happens to phosphate when renal excretion is severely impaired?
cards.back: Phosphate may accumulate; kidney function and other factors must be assessed.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Fasting plasma glucose?
cards.back: 70-99 mg/dL after at least 8 hours without calories. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: Why must fasting status be checked when interpreting glucose?
cards.back: Food intake affects glucose; fasting and random measurements use different interpretive criteria.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Hemoglobin A1c, usual nondiabetic category?
cards.back: Below 5.7%. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: What time period does hemoglobin A1c broadly reflect?
cards.back: Roughly the preceding 2-3 months, weighted toward recent weeks; altered red-cell turnover can distort it.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Blood urea nitrogen?
cards.back: About 7-20 mg/dL. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: Why is BUN not a kidney-only marker?
cards.back: Hydration, protein intake, gastrointestinal bleeding, and tissue breakdown can affect BUN as well as kidney function.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Adult serum creatinine?
cards.back: About 0.6-1.3 mg/dL. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: Why can a seemingly normal creatinine conceal reduced kidney function?
cards.back: Creatinine production depends on muscle mass; a low-muscle-mass patient may have reduced filtration with a modest creatinine.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Serum albumin?
cards.back: 3.5-5.0 g/dL. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: Why is albumin alone an imperfect nutrition marker?
cards.back: Inflammation, liver synthesis, fluid status, and protein loss also affect albumin.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Serum total protein?
cards.back: About 6.0-8.3 g/dL. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: What are the main protein groups included in total serum protein?
cards.back: Albumin and globulins.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Total bilirubin?
cards.back: About 0.2-1.2 mg/dL. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: What visible finding can accompany elevated bilirubin?
cards.back: Jaundice, or yellowing of the skin and sclerae; the cause requires further evaluation.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Direct bilirubin?
cards.back: About 0-0.3 mg/dL. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: What does direct bilirubin largely measure?
cards.back: Conjugated bilirubin, which has been processed by the liver and is water soluble.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for AST?
cards.back: About 10-40 units/L. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: Why is AST less liver-specific than ALT?
cards.back: AST is present in several tissues, including skeletal and cardiac muscle, as well as the liver.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for ALT?
cards.back: About 7-56 units/L. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: What does an elevated ALT commonly suggest?
cards.back: Hepatocellular injury; ALT does not by itself measure overall liver function or establish a cause.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Adult alkaline phosphatase?
cards.back: About 44-147 units/L. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: Which two major tissue sources can raise alkaline phosphatase?
cards.back: Liver or biliary tissue and bone; age and pregnancy also affect the reference interval.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Serum amylase?
cards.back: About 30-110 units/L. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: Why is amylase not specific for pancreatic disease?
cards.back: Salivary glands also produce amylase, and other conditions can raise it.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Serum lipase?
cards.back: About 0-160 units/L; strongly assay-dependent. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: Which pancreatic enzyme is generally more specific than amylase for acute pancreatitis?
cards.back: Lipase; interpretation requires symptoms, assay limits, and clinical context.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for White blood cell count?
cards.back: 4,500-11,000 cells/microliter. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: Can a normal WBC count exclude infection?
cards.back: No. Infection may occur with a normal, high, or low WBC count.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Platelet count?
cards.back: 150,000-400,000 platelets/microliter. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: What is the main role of platelets in hemostasis?
cards.back: They adhere, activate, and aggregate to form the initial platelet plug.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Hemoglobin, typical adult male interval?
cards.back: About 13.5-17.5 g/dL. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: What does hemoglobin concentration help assess?
cards.back: The blood's oxygen-carrying protein concentration; a low value can indicate anemia but does not identify its cause.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Hemoglobin, typical adult female interval?
cards.back: About 12.0-16.0 g/dL. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: How can acute hemorrhage initially affect measured hemoglobin?
cards.back: The concentration may initially appear near baseline because whole blood is lost; trends and clinical findings matter.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Hematocrit, typical adult male interval?
cards.back: About 41-53%. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: What does hematocrit measure?
cards.back: The fraction of blood volume occupied by red blood cells.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Hematocrit, typical adult female interval?
cards.back: About 36-46%. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: How can dehydration affect hematocrit?
cards.back: Reduced plasma volume can increase hematocrit by hemoconcentration.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Mean corpuscular volume?
cards.back: 80-100 fL. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: What does a low MCV suggest about red-cell size?
cards.back: Microcytosis: average red cells are smaller than the reference interval.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Mean corpuscular hemoglobin?
cards.back: About 27-33 pg/cell. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: What does MCH quantify?
cards.back: The average mass of hemoglobin in one red blood cell.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration?
cards.back: About 32-36 g/dL. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: What does MCHC quantify?
cards.back: The average hemoglobin concentration within the red-cell volume.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Reticulocyte percentage in adults?
cards.back: About 0.5-2.5%. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: What can an increased reticulocyte count suggest?
cards.back: An increased marrow response to red-cell loss or destruction; anemia may require a corrected count or production index.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Prothrombin time without anticoagulation?
cards.back: About 11-13.5 seconds; reagent-dependent. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: Which pathways does PT primarily assess?
cards.back: The extrinsic and common coagulation pathways.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for INR without anticoagulation?
cards.back: About 0.8-1.1. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: Why is INR used rather than raw PT for monitoring warfarin?
cards.back: INR standardizes PT for differences in thromboplastin reagents; therapeutic targets depend on the indication.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for aPTT without anticoagulation?
cards.back: About 25-35 seconds; laboratory-dependent. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: Which pathways does aPTT primarily assess?
cards.back: The intrinsic and common coagulation pathways.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Fibrinogen?
cards.back: About 200-400 mg/dL. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: What is fibrinogen's role in coagulation?
cards.back: Thrombin converts soluble fibrinogen into fibrin, which helps stabilize the clot.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Arterial pH?
cards.back: 7.35-7.45, unitless. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: What does arterial pH below 7.35 indicate?
cards.back: Acidemia; determine respiratory and metabolic contributions rather than assuming a single cause.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Arterial PaCO2?
cards.back: 35-45 mm Hg. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: Which acid-base component is primarily reflected by PaCO2?
cards.back: The respiratory component; carbon dioxide retention tends to lower pH.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Arterial bicarbonate?
cards.back: 22-26 mEq/L. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: Which acid-base component is primarily reflected by bicarbonate?
cards.back: The metabolic component; reduced bicarbonate tends to lower pH.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Arterial PaO2 in a young adult at sea level on room air?
cards.back: About 80-100 mm Hg. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: Why must age, altitude, and inspired oxygen be considered with PaO2?
cards.back: Each changes the expected arterial oxygen partial pressure, so a single interval is not universal.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Pulse oximetry in a healthy adult at sea level?
cards.back: Usually 95-100%. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: Why does a normal SpO2 not prove adequate ventilation?
cards.back: Pulse oximetry estimates oxygen saturation, not carbon dioxide removal; hypoventilation can occur despite an acceptable reading.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Resting adult pulse?
cards.back: 60-100 beats/minute. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: What is adult resting tachycardia by a common definition?
cards.back: A resting heart rate above 100 beats/minute; determine the cause and clinical significance.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Resting adult respiratory rate?
cards.back: Common nursing interval: 12-20 breaths/minute; some references use 12-18. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: What does respiratory rate alone fail to describe?
cards.back: Breath depth, effort, pattern, and gas exchange; assess these as well as the rate.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Typical adult oral temperature?
cards.back: About 97.7-99.1 degrees F; varies with site and time. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: Why must the measurement site accompany a temperature reading?
cards.back: Oral, axillary, rectal, and other measurements differ and should not be treated as interchangeable.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Adult normal blood pressure category?
cards.back: Systolic below 120 mm Hg and diastolic below 80 mm Hg; low values still need context. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: What does the upper number in a blood pressure reading represent?
cards.back: Systolic arterial pressure, the peak pressure associated with ventricular contraction.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Urine specific gravity?
cards.back: About 1.005-1.030. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: What does urine specific gravity estimate?
cards.back: Urine density relative to water, reflecting concentration; glucose or protein can also increase it.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Urine pH?
cards.back: About 4.5-8.0. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: Why does urine pH differ substantially from blood pH?
cards.back: The kidneys excrete acid or base, and diet, medications, and infection can alter urinary pH.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Urine red blood cells on microscopy?
cards.back: Usually 0-2 cells per high-power field. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: Why should collection contamination be considered with urine red cells?
cards.back: Menstruation or traumatic collection can introduce blood unrelated to intrinsic urinary disease.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Urine white blood cells on microscopy?
cards.back: Usually 0-5 cells per high-power field. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: Does pyuria alone prove a bacterial urinary tract infection?
cards.back: No. White cells indicate inflammation and must be interpreted with symptoms, collection quality, and other testing.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Serum osmolality?
cards.back: About 275-295 mOsm/kg. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: Which solutes are commonly used in calculated serum osmolality?
cards.back: Sodium, glucose, and BUN; with US units, a common estimate is 2 times sodium + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8.

cards.front: What is a commonly used adult reference range for Blood lactate?
cards.back: About 0.5-2.0 mmol/L, commonly reported this way in US labs. Use the reporting laboratory or stated exam reference range.

cards.front: Does elevated lactate always mean sepsis?
cards.back: No. Tissue hypoperfusion, seizures, some drugs, impaired clearance, and other causes can raise lactate.
